description: The European Union governs **450 million citizens**, but its functioning is often seen as a black box. This is how a European law really comes about, and who decides what.

hero.hook: 27 countries, only one common rule: delve into the most complex mechanics of world politics.

blocks.text: The **European Union** is the most advanced experiment in union between countries in modern history. It transformed a continent ravaged by wars into a vast common economic and political space.

However, its operation is often perceived as a black box by the 450 million citizens it concerns. Understanding how a decision is born in Brussels allows you to better follow major European issues, from ecology to digital security.

The EU operates on a system of three institutions which must agree among themselves. The ****European Council, made up of the heads of state of member countries, sets the main political guidelines at summits, without writing laws itself.

blocks.caption: Heads of state meet at the European Council to set the main guidelines.

blocks.text: The power to make laws is shared between the , which represents the 27 governments, and the **European Parliament**, the only institution elected directly by citizens. The latter ensures the democratic legitimacy of the system. [[EU Council]]

Finally, the  plays the executive role. She is the only one who can propose a new law, an exclusive called . It also ensures that countries respect common rules. [[European Commission]] [[The European Commission and the monopoly of legislative initiative]]

The European Parliament officially sits in two cities: Brussels and Strasbourg. Every month, its 705 deputies and all their staff take a special train to reach Alsace, a costly but symbolic ritual of Franco-German reconciliation.

sections.title: Three powers, none alone in control

blocks.text: A European law follows a specific path, called the ordinary legislative procedure. It all starts with a proposal from the Commission, often after a long phase of consultation with experts and . [[interest groups]]

The text is then examined by the Parliament and the Council of the EU. If they do not agree, a shuttle is organized between the two institutions. As a last resort, a  is brought together to find a compromise. [[conciliation committee]]

Once adopted, the law can take two forms: the **regulation**, which applies directly and equally in all countries, or the **directive**, which sets a goal but lets each country choose how to achieve it.
The Court of Justice of the EU has had to resolve sometimes unusual conflicts, such as the famous “banana war”, a dispute over customs tariffs on tropical fruits which lasted more than twenty years.

sections.title: How a European law is born

blocks.text: The EU does not have unlimited power: it can only act in the areas that countries have entrusted to it. Certain skills belong to it alone, such as the management of the single currency or the rules of international trade.

blocks.caption: The European Union shares its powers between several decision-making levels.

blocks.text: Other skills are shared with countries, such as the environment or transport: this is where the EU acts most often, but only when its action is more effective than that of each isolated country.

Finally, sensitive subjects such as taxation, health or defense remain almost entirely managed by each country, and often require the unanimous agreement of all members via . It is this blockage which explains why the EU can easily sanction a large company, but sometimes struggles to agree on a common position in the face of an international crisis. [[Unanimity in the Council of the EU]]

sections.title: What the EU can and cannot do

blocks.text: The image of a Europe led by “unelected technocrats” deserves to be qualified. The heads of the Commission are appointed by democratically elected governments, then validated by Parliament. The European administration also remains modest: around 60,000 agents to manage an entire continent, fewer than the city of Paris alone.

The challenge of feeling distanced from citizens remains real. To respond, the EU created the European Citizens' Initiative, which allows one million citizens to ask the Commission to study a new law.

The 2020 pandemic marked a turning point: for the first time, member countries agreed to borrow together on the financial markets with the Next Generation EU plan. This transition from a market union to a more united union shows a Europe that continues to evolve.

The European Union is based on a sharing of power between 27 countries and three institutions, none of which can decide alone. This complex system guarantees peace and stability, but often remains slow in the face of rapid crises.

title: The EU: how does it really work?
